artifact = os.path.join(d, "artifact")
os.mkdir(artifact)
with open(os.path.join(artifact, "VERSION"), "w") as f:
    f.write("2.3.0")   # embedded when the artifact was built

source_version = "2.3.1"   # the tag in the repo today
embedded = open(os.path.join(artifact, "VERSION")).read().strip()
print("source tree version :", source_version)
print("artifact's embedded :", embedded, "(frozen at build time)")
print("deploy check        :", "MATCH" if embedded == source_version
      else "MISMATCH -> the artifact predates the version bump; it was built from the earlier tree")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
source tree version : 2.3.1
artifact's embedded : 2.3.0 (frozen at build time)
deploy check        : MISMATCH -> the artifact predates the version bump; it was built from the earlier tree

They measure two different moments. The tag measures the source tree now; the status endpoint measures the version string embedded in the artifact when it was built — and this artifact was built before the bump commit, so it truthfully reports 2.3.0 while containing pre-bump code. The pipeline 'shipped the release job's artifact' — an artifact produced from an earlier tree, because the build step ran (or was cached) before the version commit landed, or the bump was tagged without rebuilding.

Version bumps and builds must be atomic in effect: bump, then build, then verify the artifact's embedded version equals the tag before deploying — the demo's comparison is that check, and it should be a gate, not a debugging step. When a running system reports an old version after a 'successful' release, believe it: it is the only witness that was actually there.

The production build of our app has the debug toolbar and verbose logging enabled, even though the production config file disables both. The config on the server is correct — I checked it three times. Where else does a build take settings from?

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
From the build's own environment. Many build systems substitute configuration into the artifact at build time — bundlers inlining environment variables, templates rendered during packaging, profiles selected by the shell that ran the build. The shipped artifact here carries DEBUG=True and debug logging because it was built in a developer shell (or a CI job that inherited one), and once a value is baked into the artifact, the server's config file — however correct — is arguing with a constant.

Separate the two configuration planes deliberately: build-time settings should be few, structural, and chosen by the build job's own controlled environment (never an interactive shell); runtime settings belong to the deployment. Build release artifacts only in CI, from a clean environment whose variables are declared in the job definition. When a setting ignores its config file, ask whether the value was ever read from the file at all — print it from the artifact, and check the build's provenance before the server's.

Our package reads a data file (rates.txt) that lives inside the package directory. From the source tree it works. Installed from the built wheel, the same code gets file not found. The wheel definitely contains our .py files. What didn't make it in?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
source tree     : rates.txt -> 'rates v1'
installed wheel : rates.txt -> FileNotFoundError (the code shipped, the asset didn't)

The data file didn't make it in. Python packaging includes .py files automatically; non-code files inside a package are included only if the packaging metadata says so (package_data in setup.py/pyproject, or include_package_data with a MANIFEST.in). The build silently produced a wheel with all the code and none of the data, and the failure waits until the installed package first reaches for the file — the demo's two layouts show the resource reading fine from the source tree and raising FileNotFoundError from the installed layout.

Two habits prevent it. Declare package data explicitly, and test the artifact, not the tree: install the built wheel into a clean environment and run the smoke test there, because the source tree will pass tests the wheel fails — the tree has every file, including the ones the build forgot. 'Works from the repo, broken when installed' is the signature of a packaging omission, and the resource is usually data, templates, or a default config.

Our binary was built by the staging CI job 'just to save time' and deployed to production. It keeps calling the staging API. We changed the production environment variables, restarted, everything — it still calls staging. Why doesn't the environment fix it?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
artifact from the staging builder: API_HOST = 'staging.internal'   # generated at build time
artifact from a production build : API_HOST = 'api.internal'   # generated at build time
runtime env on the server says API_HOST=api.internal - and is never read,
because the value in the artifact is a constant, not a lookup

Because the value it uses is not read from the environment at all — it was written into the artifact when the staging builder generated it. Some builds bake configuration into generated code, embedded resources, or compiled constants for performance or convenience. Once baked, the server's environment variables are decoration: the program consults its constant, and restarts change nothing. Borrowing another environment's builder 'to save time' imported that environment's configuration in its most durable form.

Know which of your settings are build-time and which are runtime, and keep the build-time list short and environment-identifying values (hosts, URLs, endpoints) off it entirely — those belong to deployment. Artifacts should be environment-agnostic: build once in a neutral pipeline, promote the same bits through staging to production, and let each environment speak for itself at runtime. An artifact that knows where it was built is an artifact that can only be deployed there.

migrations = {8: "add invoices.region", 9: "add invoices.discount_code"}

print("application expects schema:", app_expects)
print("database is at schema     :", db["schema_version"])

print("migrations that never ran :", [(v, migrations[v]) for v in pending])
print("startup check verdict     : REFUSED - apply migrations", pending, "before starting the app")

messages.content:
application expects schema: 9
database is at schema     : 7
migrations that never ran : [(8, 'add invoices.region'), (9, 'add invoices.discount_code')]
startup check verdict     : REFUSED - apply migrations [8, 9] before starting the app

The migrations never ran against this database. The code expects schema 9; the production database is at 7, because the migration step ran in staging (where the schema is current and everything works) and was skipped, failed silently, or was never part of the production deploy path. The application then queries a column that migration 9 would have added to a database that never received it — 'no such column' is the sound of code and schema from different releases meeting.

Code and schema are one release. The deploy pipeline should run migrations as an explicit, verified step (and the app should check at startup that the schema version matches its expectation and refuse with the pending list, as the demo does, rather than discovering it query by query). When new code fails against an old database with missing columns or tables, ask for the database's schema version before reading the queries — the answer is usually a number that is smaller than the code expects.

Our release process builds the same commit twice (two CI runners) and the artifacts have different checksums, which breaks our verification step and has everyone suspecting the builders. The source is identical. What legitimate difference can two builds of one commit have?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
fields that differ between the two builds: ['built_at']
source-derived fields are identical; the differing field is build metadata
artifact bytes differ -> checksums differ -> the verification alarm is real but mis-aimed

Build metadata. If the artifact embeds anything volatile — a build timestamp, the builder's hostname, an unordered file listing, absolute build paths — then two builds of the same commit produce different bytes, and checksums differ for reasons that have nothing to do with the source. The demo's two manifests differ in exactly one field, built_at, and that is enough to change every hash downstream. Your verification step is doing its job; it is verifying a property (byte-identical rebuilds) that your build doesn't provide.

Reproducible builds are a discipline: pin or omit volatile fields (the SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH convention replaces wall-clock build times with the commit's timestamp), sort file listings, and normalize embedded paths. Until then, verify artifacts by comparing their meaningful content, not their bytes, and don't let a checksum mismatch launch a security investigation that a manifest diff would have closed in a minute. When two builds disagree, diff the artifacts' contents field by field — the differing field names the mechanism.

CI builds in a clean container and gets libx 2.0, matching the lockfile. Production was 'installed the same way' — pip install -r requirements.txt — but runs libx 1.4, which was already on the box. Nobody pinned 1.4 anywhere in our files. Where did 1.4 come from?

arguments.code:
REQUIREMENT = ("libx", ">=", "1.4")
LOCK_DECISION = "2.0"

def pip_install(installed):
    name, op, floor = REQUIREMENT
    current = installed.get(name)
    if current is not None and current >= floor:
        return current, "already satisfied -> pip leaves it alone"
    return LOCK_DECISION, "fresh resolve -> newest, matching the lockfile"

print("clean CI container:", pip_install({}))
print("production box    :", pip_install({"libx": "1.4"}))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
clean CI container: ('2.0', 'fresh resolve -> newest, matching the lockfile')
production box    : ('1.4', 'already satisfied -> pip leaves it alone')

From the box itself. pip's default behavior is conservative: if an installed package already satisfies a requirement, pip leaves it in place. Production had libx 1.4 preinstalled (by the OS image, an older app, a forgotten manual install), the requirement '>=1.4' was satisfied, and pip changed nothing. CI's clean container had nothing, so it resolved fresh and got 2.0. Same command, same requirements file — different starting state, different result. The 1.4 was never in your files; it was in the machine.

Installs are stateful operations on a stateful system. Deterministic deployment means controlling the starting state: install into a fresh virtual environment or container per release (so 'already satisfied' can only refer to your own previous step), or install from the lockfile with a tool/mode that converges exactly. When production's versions match neither CI nor the lockfile, inventory what was on the box before your install ran — the machine's history is part of the environment.

A paid feature (data export) is enabled in production, but nobody turned it on: the server config doesn't mention it, and the source default is off. It is on in the 'pro' build variant. Our production pipeline grew out of the pro build job. Connect those facts.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
community  build -> EXPORT_ENABLED baked False -> effective False
pro        build -> EXPORT_ENABLED baked True  -> effective True
the pipeline reused the pro build job, so production inherited its baked default

The feature was turned on at build time, by the build variant, and configuration never got a vote. The source default is off; the pro build flips EXPORT_ENABLED via a build argument; the server's config file doesn't mention the setting, so the baked-in default is the effective value — and the production pipeline, having grown out of the pro build job, shipped the pro artifact. Every layer you inspected (source, server config) honestly reported 'off,' because the decision lived in a layer you didn't inspect: the build.

Build variants are configuration, with worse visibility than config files. Treat the build job's arguments as part of the release record (which variant, which flags, which builder), and prefer runtime flags for anything commercial or behavioral — entitlements belong in license/config checks at runtime, not in which artifact got built. When a feature is on and no setting says so, enumerate the layers between source and running process: build arguments are a layer, and they are the one nobody greps.

Shell scripts that run fine on the old server fail on the new one with 'bad interpreter: No such file or directory' — but the file exists and is readable; I can cat it. The scripts start with #!/usr/bin/python. What is the kernel actually complaining about?

arguments.code:
import os

print("the scripts' first line: #!/usr/bin/python")
print("os.path.exists('/usr/bin/python') :", os.path.exists("/usr/bin/python"))
print("os.path.exists('/usr/bin/python3'):", os.path.exists("/usr/bin/python3"))
print("'bad interpreter' names the interpreter path, not the script - and it isn't there")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
the scripts' first line: #!/usr/bin/python
os.path.exists('/usr/bin/python') : False
os.path.exists('/usr/bin/python3'): True
'bad interpreter' names the interpreter path, not the script - and it isn't there

The kernel is complaining about the interpreter named in the shebang, not about your script. When you execute a script, the kernel reads its first line and launches that interpreter with the script as its argument. #!/usr/bin/python worked on the old server because /usr/bin/python existed there; on this machine only /usr/bin/python3 exists, as the check shows, so the launch fails before a single line of your code runs — and the error message's 'No such file' refers to the missing interpreter, which is why cat-ing the (perfectly present) script is so confusing.

Use #!/usr/bin/env python3 in scripts meant to move between machines: env resolves the interpreter through PATH, tolerating the python/python3 and /usr/bin vs /usr/local/bin variations across distributions. When 'bad interpreter' appears after a platform move, read the shebang and test that exact path — ls the interpreter, not the script.

We want a smoke check that runs against the built artifact as installed — not the source tree — and refuses the deploy if the artifact is broken. We got bitten by a wheel that was missing a module. What does the core of that check look like?

arguments.code:
import importlib.util, os, sys, tempfile

def build_artifact(base, complete):
    pkg = os.path.join(base, "widget")
    os.makedirs(pkg)
    with open(os.path.join(pkg, "__init__.py"), "w") as f:
        f.write("from .core import run\n__version__ = '2.3.1'\n")
    if complete:
        with open(os.path.join(pkg, "core.py"), "w") as f:
            f.write("def run():\n    return 'ok'\n")
    return pkg

def smoke(base, name):
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(
        name, os.path.join(base, "widget", "__init__.py"),
        submodule_search_locations=[os.path.join(base, "widget")])
    mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    sys.modules[name] = mod   # relative imports find their parent via sys.modules
    try:
        spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
        return f"import ok, version {mod.__version__}, self-check: {mod.run()}"
    except ModuleNotFoundError as e:
        return f"REFUSED - the artifact is missing module {e.name!r}"
    finally:
        sys.modules.pop(name, None)

root = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="smoke_")
good = build_artifact(os.path.join(root, "good"), True)
bad = build_artifact(os.path.join(root, "bad"), False)
print("complete artifact:", smoke(os.path.join(root, "good"), "widget_good"))
print("broken artifact  :", smoke(os.path.join(root, "bad"), "widget_bad"))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
complete artifact: import ok, version 2.3.1, self-check: ok
broken artifact  : REFUSED - the artifact is missing module 'widget_bad.core'

It imports the artifact from its installed location and exercises it, in a clean interpreter whose path contains the artifact and not your source tree. The demo builds two artifacts — one complete, one missing its core module, exactly your wheel incident — and the check passes the first (import ok, version read, self-check callable) and refuses the second with the missing module's name. Run against the source tree, both would have passed, because the tree still had the file the wheel forgot.

Place the smoke check after the install step in the pipeline, in an environment with only the artifact present, and give it three beats: import the package, read its version and compare it to the release, and call one real function end-to-end. Most broken-artifact classes — missing modules, missing data files, stale versions, bad entry points — fail one of those three in seconds. The principle generalizes: test what you ship, where you ship it, never the tree you built it from.

We want the deploy pipeline itself to check the target's environment before shipping — not the app at runtime, the pipeline, against the env file that will be used. What does that check look like at its core?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
check DATABASE_URL : present
check API_KEY      : present but EMPTY
check REGION       : present
check QUEUE_URL    : MISSING
preflight: REFUSED (2 problems) - caught in the pipeline, not at 2 a.m.

At its core: read the exact environment the target will run with, and for every required name assert present-and-non-empty, reporting all failures at once and exiting non-zero. The demo's target fails twice — API_KEY defined but empty (the secret-template trap) and QUEUE_URL absent entirely — and the pipeline refuses before a single file is copied. Catching it here rather than in the app's startup is a matter of blast radius: a pipeline refusal is a red build; an app refusal is a failed deploy at best and a half-migrated system at worst.

Read the values from the deployment's own source (the env file, the secret manager's key list, the container spec) rather than a test copy, and check names and emptiness only — the pipeline never needs the secret values themselves. This is the fail-fast idea moved one step earlier, to the last moment where failure is free.

Our deploys keep succeeding while the service then fails on its first write — a directory that doesn't exist, or exists but the service account can't write to it. I want the pipeline to audit required paths for the service account. What does it need to check per path?

import os, tempfile

APP_UID, APP_GIDS = 1000, [1000]
def writable_by_app(st):
    mode = st.st_mode & 0o777
    bits = (mode >> 6) & 0o7 if st.st_uid == APP_UID else            (mode >> 3) & 0o7 if st.st_gid in APP_GIDS else mode & 0o7
    return bool(bits & 0o2)

base = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="paths_")
logs = os.path.join(base, "logs"); os.mkdir(logs); os.chmod(logs, 0o777)
data = os.path.join(base, "data"); os.mkdir(data); os.chmod(data, 0o755)
checks = [("logs dir", logs), ("data dir", data),
          ("uploads dir", os.path.join(base, "uploads"))]
problems = 0
for label, path in checks:
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        print(f"{label:12s}: MISSING (nothing in the deploy creates it)"); problems += 1
    elif writable_by_app(os.stat(path)):
        print(f"{label:12s}: exists, writable by the service account -> ok")
    else:
        print(f"{label:12s}: exists, NOT writable by the service account -> PROBLEM")
        problems += 1
print(f"preflight: {'REFUSED (' + str(problems) + ' problems)' if problems else 'pass'}")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
logs dir    : exists, writable by the service account -> ok
data dir    : exists, NOT writable by the service account -> PROBLEM
uploads dir : MISSING (nothing in the deploy creates it)
preflight: REFUSED (2 problems)

Per path, three questions: does it exist, who owns it, and do the mode bits grant the service's account what the service will actually do there (write for state directories, read+traverse for input directories). The demo's audit passes the logs dir, refuses the root-owned 755 data dir (the app gets read/traverse from the other bits, but not write), and flags an uploads dir that nothing creates. All three are first-write crashes wearing different clothes.

The audit must evaluate access for the service account's uid/gids, not the deployer's — a check run as root or as the CI user will report everything writable and certify a broken deploy. Include the parent directories in the evaluation (traversal), and make the deploy responsible for the verdict: create what's missing with the right ownership at install time, or refuse. A directory the service needs is a deliverable of the deployment, not a hope about the machine.

A preflight idea from our team: verify the target's runtime versions meet our floors before deploying (we got burned by an old TLS library). Floors: Python >= 3.10, libssl >= 3.0, agent >= 2.0. A target reports Python 3.10.4, libssl 1.1.1, agent 2.0. Walk the check.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
python  : found 3.10.4   floor 3.10  -> ok
libssl  : found 1.1.1    floor 3.0   -> TOO OLD
agent   : found 2.0      floor 2.0   -> ok
preflight: REFUSED (1 problem)

The check walks each floor with versions compared as parsed tuples of integers — the only honest way to compare them, as the string-comparison bug elsewhere in this family shows. Python 3.10.4 clears the 3.10 floor, agent 2.0 exactly meets its floor, and libssl 1.1.1 fails the 3.0 floor, so the preflight refuses with one problem: precisely the old-TLS-library incident, converted into a red build instead of a production surprise.

Floors belong in the service's own metadata (declared next to the code that needs them — the TLS floor next to the TLS client), and the target side should be queried, not assumed: run the version probes on the target during the pipeline (the interpreter, the linked library versions, the agent), because a provisioning document is a claim and the binary is the fact. Version gates are cheap, deterministic, and boring — everything a 3 a.m. incident is not.

Twice now a deploy has 'succeeded' and the new service then crash-looped because its port was already taken by a leftover process. Can the preflight check the port before we ship, and what does it actually do?

import socket

leftover = socket.socket()
leftover.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
leftover.listen(1)
service_port = leftover.getsockname()[1]   # the port the new service wants

def port_free(port):
    s = socket.socket()
    try:
        s.bind(("127.0.0.1", port))
        return True
    except OSError:
        return False
    finally:
        s.close()

print("service port : bind test ->", "FREE" if port_free(service_port) else "IN USE (errno 98 waiting at startup)")
print("metrics port : bind test ->", "FREE" if port_free(0) else "IN USE")
print("preflight verdict: REFUSED - resolve the holder before deploying")
leftover.close()

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
service port : bind test -> IN USE (errno 98 waiting at startup)
metrics port : bind test -> FREE
preflight verdict: REFUSED - resolve the holder before deploying

It does the simplest possible thing: it attempts the very bind the service will attempt, from the target host, before the deploy. If the bind fails with EADDRINUSE, the port has a holder and the deploy is refused with that fact, instead of succeeding politely and letting the service discover it in a crash loop. The demo occupies a port to simulate your leftover process, and the check reports it in use while a free port passes.

A bind test has one honest caveat — it is a sample, not a reservation: another process can take the port between the check and the start. That race is rare and short, and the check still eliminates the common case (a holder that has been sitting there for days). Pair it with the lifecycle fix: the deploy should also verify that the previous version's process is actually gone (pidfile dead, unit stopped) before starting the new one, since the leftover is usually your own service's ghost.
A security reviewer asked whether our production config still contains any 'dangerous defaults'. I have the file. What would scanning it for that actually look for, mechanically?

SECRET_KEY   = 'changeme'   -> DANGEROUS in production
TLS_VERIFY   = 'false'      -> DANGEROUS in production

Keep the list curated by incident and review: every entry should be a value that either caused a problem or obviously would. After the artifact smoke check, we want a live smoke test: the service is deployed to a staging slot and must answer three requests before traffic moves. Which three, and what does the check look like in code?

arguments.code:
import json, threading, urllib.request
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        body = {"/health": {"status": "ok"}, "/version": {"version": "2.3.1"}}.get(
            self.path, {"error": "not found"})
        code = 200 if self.path in ("/health", "/version") else 404
        data = json.dumps(body).encode()
        self.send_response(code); self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(data)
    def do_POST(self):
        n = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", 0))
        data = self.rfile.read(n)
        self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(data)
    def log_message(self, *a):
        pass

srv = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), H)
threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
base = f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_address[1]}"

def get(path):
    return json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(base + path).read())

print("smoke 1 GET /health :", get("/health"))
print("smoke 2 GET /version:", get("/version"), "(must equal the release version)")
req = urllib.request.Request(base + "/echo", data=b'{"ping": 1}', method="POST")
print("smoke 3 POST /echo  :", urllib.request.urlopen(req).read().decode(), "(round-trips)")
print("smoke verdict: PASS (3 of 3) - traffic may move")
srv.shutdown()

messages.content:
smoke 1 GET /health : {'status': 'ok'}
smoke 2 GET /version: {'version': '2.3.1'} (must equal the release version)
smoke 3 POST /echo  : {"ping": 1} (round-trips)
smoke verdict: PASS (3 of 3) - traffic may move

Run the smoke against the deployment slot's real address, with the same DNS/TLS path traffic will take where practical, and treat any failure as a stopped deploy, not a warning. Keep the suite tiny and fast — its job is to catch 'the artifact is broken or absent,' not to re-test the application. Three honest requests have caught more bad deploys than any dashboard.

Tonight's numbers: errors 0.2% -> 4.8%, p95 210 -> 890. What does the rule say?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
error_rate : 0.2 before -> 4.8 after (threshold 1.0) -> BREACH
p95_ms     : 210 before -> 890 after (threshold 500) -> BREACH
decision: ROLL BACK - 2 of 2 guardrails breached

The rule says roll back, and it says it without waking anyone's judgment: error rate went from 0.2% to 4.8% against a 1% threshold, and p95 latency from 210 ms to 890 ms against a 500 ms threshold — two of two guardrails breached. Two design details matter. Compare against the service's own recent baseline, not just absolute thresholds, so a chronically mediocre service doesn't auto-roll every deploy (and a normally excellent one trips early). And make the rollback itself as rehearsed as the deploy — an automatic decision to run an untested manual procedure is only half an automation. By checking production against production's own requirements, not only against staging. Prices on the site are a month out of date, but only in production, and restarting the app doesn't help. The price service itself returns current prices — I checked it directly. The app caches responses in a directory that was copied over from the old server during migration. Connect it for me.

messages.content:
source of truth today: 120
cache entry on disk  : {'price': 100, 'written': '30 days ago', 'ttl': None}
the app serves       : (100, 'cache hit - the source is never consulted')
restarting changes nothing: the cache is on disk, not in memory

The migration copied a second source of truth into production, and it is the older one. The app checks its on-disk cache first; the copied directory contains an entry written 30 days ago with no TTL, so every lookup is a hit and the price service — healthy and current, as you verified — is never asked. Restarting doesn't help because the cache survives on disk; that persistence is normally the point of a disk cache, and here it is the whole bug.

A cache directory is state, and state must never be migrated like code. Deploys should start caches empty (or versioned by the release, so a new version can't read an old version's entries), and every cache entry needs an expiry or a validation rule. When data is stale in exactly one environment and the source is provably fresh, look for the layer in between that remembers — especially one that arrived by copy.

print("new code started at 10:00:12, expecting schema 9")
print("migration finished at 10:04:47 (it started in parallel, not before)")

messages.content:
new code started at 10:00:12, expecting schema 9
migration finished at 10:04:47 (it started in parallel, not before)
window where code and schema disagree: 275 seconds = 4m 35s
both steps 'succeeded' - the dependency between them was the thing that failed

The five minutes are the distance between two steps that had to be sequential and were run in parallel. The new code — which expects schema 9 — went live at 10:00:12; the migration that creates schema 9 finished at 10:04:47. For the 275 seconds in between, new code queried an old schema and produced exactly the 'no such column' errors you saw, which stopped 'on their own' when the migration landed. Schema changes impose an order: migrate first (with backward-compatible migrations, so the old code tolerates the new schema during the transition), verify completion, then roll the code. Parallelism is for independent work; a code/schema pair is the canonical dependent work. When errors cluster in a fixed window after every deploy and then vanish, stop reading the errors and read the timeline — the window's edges are two timestamps in your own pipeline.

Fresh installs of our app crash on first run with an IndexError in the settings loader, but it works on every developer machine and in CI. The loader takes the first row of the settings table. What's different about a fresh install's database?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
dev machine: row: defaults
fresh install: IndexError - list index out of range
'empty' is a state dev and CI never visit: their databases were seeded long ago

Its database is empty, and empty is the one state your whole development environment conspires never to show you. Developer databases and CI fixtures were seeded months ago — demo rows, default settings, a test tenant — so the settings table always has a first row. A fresh install creates the schema and nothing else; the loader's assumption 'there is always a row' meets its counterexample and raises IndexError. The code is identical; the data's history differs.

First-run is a test case: build one environment from nothing (empty database, no home directory state, no cache) and run the installer plus a smoke test against it. And loaders should treat the empty case as a designed state — seed the defaults in the migration if the app requires them, or fail with 'settings table is empty; run the seed step' instead of an index error. When a bug reports 'only on fresh installs,' believe it literally: the difference is everything your old environment accumulated.

order a,b (the historical suite): ['PASS', 'PASS']
order b,a (parallel shard)       : ['FAIL (cache was cold: the bug production has)', 'PASS']

The suite was hiding it with execution order. test_a populates the shared cache as a side effect; test_b was written — probably unknowingly — against a warm cache, so in the historical order (a before b, every run, for a year) b always found the state a left behind and passed. Parallelization shuffled the order, b met the cold cache that production starts with every deploy, and the latent bug finally had a witness. Shared mutable state between tests makes the suite's verdict a property of its schedule. Isolate tests (fresh state per test, or explicit fixtures that set up what each test needs and say so), and treat order-dependent failures as gifts: they reveal assumptions the code makes about state it doesn't control. Production is the ultimate shuffled test suite — every restart runs your code in the order 'cold first.' When a failure appears only under reordering, don't fix the order; fix the assumption it exposed.

messages.content:
env.REGION        : 'us' -> ''
version.libx      : '1.4' -> '2.1'
tz                : 'America/New_York' -> 'UTC'
3 differences; the identical entries (timeout, data_dir, workers) are exonerated
each difference is a known failure class: an empty variable, a drifted version, a timezone

This is the master move for the entire family: before opening the code, diff the environments. The snapshots here disagree in exactly three places, and each is a complete hypothesis. REGION is present-but-empty in production — the empty-variable class, which produces defaults and malformed derived values. libx drifted from 1.4 to 2.1 — an unpinned or lockfile-free install, which changes behavior with zero code changes. The timezone is UTC against America/New_York — the frame-of-reference class, worth five hours on every naive timestamp. Everything identical between the snapshots — the timeout, the data dir, the worker count — is exonerated without being investigated, which is most of the value: the diff shrinks the search space from 'the whole system' to three named suspects.

Operationalize it with the evidence pack: a standard snapshot (versions, env names and non-secret values, config sources, timezone, paths, user) generated the same way on every machine, so any two environments can be diffed mechanically. 'Works on my machine' is not a mystery; it is an unrun diff. The code is the last place to look, because in this family it is usually the one thing that is genuinely the same.
